title: Mixing to be unpredictable
objectives: Find a mixed equilibrium by making the opponent indifferent.

screens.title: When Ana does not care
screens.prose: Matching pennies at £1: Ana wins £1 when the coins match, Ben when they differ. Lesson 3 found no pure equilibrium. Suppose Ben shows heads with chance $q$. Slide $q$ and watch Ana's two expected payoffs.

derive.caption: At q = {{fixed(q, 2)}}, Heads pays Ana {{fixed(2 * q - 1, 2)}} and Tails {{fixed(1 - 2 * q, 2)}} a round.

screens.question: At what $q$ does Ana earn the same from Heads and from Tails?

hints.text: Find where the two lines cross.
Heads pays $2q - 1$ and Tails $1 - 2q$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $q$ until the two dots meet.

byKey.one: At $q = 1$ Ben always shows heads, and Heads pays Ana £1 against −£1. She is far from indifferent.
byKey.zero: At $q = 0$ Tails pays Ana £1 and Heads −£1. She would show Tails.

explain.text: Heads pays $2q - 1$ and Tails pays $1 - 2q$. They are equal at $q = \tfrac12$, both 0. Any other $q$ gives Ana a side to lean on.

screens.title: Each side half the time
screens.prose: At $q = \tfrac12$ Ana is **indifferent**: both sides pay her the same. The game is symmetric, so Ana showing heads half the time makes Ben indifferent too.

derive.caption: At q = {{fixed(q, 2)}}, Heads pays Ana {{fixed(2 * q - 1, 2)}} and Tails {{fixed(1 - 2 * q, 2)}} a round.

screens.question: Both mix half and half. What does Ana expect a round, in £?

hints.text: The coins match half the time.
Ana wins £1 half the time and loses £1 half the time.

feedback.correct: 0: Ana wins and loses £1 equally often.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The coins match with chance one half.

byKey.win: £1 is a single winning round. The coins differ half the time, and then she pays £1.
byKey.half: Ana wins half the time but also pays £1 the other half: $0.5 - 0.5 = 0$.

explain.text: With both mixing half and half, the coins match with chance $\tfrac12$. Ana wins £1 or pays £1 equally often, so the game is worth 0 to her. Neither can improve by changing their mix alone, so this is a **mixed equilibrium**.

screens.title: Unequal tastes
screens.prose: Two desks pick venue X or Y. Ana is the row. Both on X pays (3, 2), both on Y pays (2, 3), apart (0, 0), in £. Each mixes so that the **other** is indifferent.
screens.question: Fill in the mixed equilibrium.

hints.text: Ben is indifferent when X and Y pay him the same against Ana's mix.
$p = \tfrac35$, $q = \tfrac25$, and each expects $3 \times \tfrac25 = \tfrac65$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r0c2: Ana's $p$ comes from Ben's payoffs: $2p = 3(1 - p)$, so $p = \tfrac35$.
byKey.r1c2: Ben's $q$ comes from Ana's payoffs: $3q = 2(1 - q)$, so $q = \tfrac25$.

explain.text: Ben is indifferent when $2p = 3(1 - p)$, so $p = \tfrac35$; Ana is indifferent when $3q = 2(1 - q)$, so $q = \tfrac25$. Each then expects $\tfrac65 = $ £1.20. That is less than either pure equilibrium, because the desks often miss each other.

screens.title: Raise Ana's prize
screens.prose: Now (X, X) pays Ana 6 instead of 3. Ben's payoffs do not change. Ben still mixes to make Ana indifferent.
screens.question: How often does Ben now play X?

hints.text: Ana is indifferent when X and Y pay her the same.
X pays her $6q$; Y pays her $2(1 - q)$.
$6q = 2 - 2q$, so $q = \tfrac14$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make Ana indifferent using her new payoffs.

byKey.same: That was Ben's mix before. Ana's payoffs changed, and they set his mix.
byKey.own: That is Ana's own mix, set by Ben's payoffs. Ben's mix solves $6q = 2(1 - q)$.
byKey.up: Ben plays X less, not more: a bigger prize for Ana on X needs less X from Ben to balance.

explain.text: $6q = 2(1 - q)$ gives $q = \tfrac14$. Ana now expects $6 \times \tfrac14 = 1.5$, up from 1.2. Ben's mix moved because Ana's payoffs moved.

screens.title: Whose payoffs set the mix
screens.prose: The same raised game: (X, X) pays Ana 6, and Ben's payoffs are as before.
screens.question: How often does Ana now play X?

options.why: You made Ana indifferent with her own payoffs. Her mix must make Ben indifferent.
You reasoned she likes X more, so plays it more. Her mix is set by Ben's payoffs, which did not change.
You weighed her prizes 6 and 1 against each other. Ana's mix solves Ben's equation $2p = 3(1 - p)$.

hints.text: Ana mixes to make Ben indifferent.
Ben's payoffs are still 2 on X and 3 on Y.
$2p = 3(1 - p)$ still gives $p = \tfrac35$.

feedback.correct: $\tfrac35$: Ben's payoffs did not change, so neither does Ana's mix.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ana's mix comes from Ben's payoffs.

byKey.b: You made Ana indifferent with her own payoffs. Her mix must make Ben indifferent.
byKey.c: Liking X more does not make Ana play it more. Her mix only has to keep Ben indifferent.

explain.text: Ana's mix exists to keep Ben indifferent, so only Ben's payoffs enter it: $2p = 3(1 - p)$, $p = \tfrac35$. Raising her own prize changed Ben's mix instead. This surprises most people, and interviewers know it.

screens.title: A crossing outside
screens.prose: Ana's payoffs: U pays 4 against L and 3 against R; D pays 1 and 2. Setting $4q + 3(1 - q) = q + 2(1 - q)$ gives $q = -\tfrac12$.

state.caption: Dashed lines mark $q = 0$ and $q = 1$; only between them is $q$ a chance.

screens.question: What does $q = -\tfrac12$ tell you?

options.text: U dominates D, so Ana never mixes

options.why: A chance cannot be negative. The lines cross outside 0 to 1, so no mix of Ben's makes Ana indifferent.
Ana mixes only when indifferent, and U beats D for every $q$ from 0 to 1.

hints.text: Where do the lines cross?
They cross at $q = -\tfrac12$, left of 0.
From 0 to 1 the U line is always higher.

feedback.correct: U beats D whatever Ben does, so Ana plays U.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the lines between $q = 0$ and $q = 1$.

byKey.b: You took the answer as a chance. A value outside 0 to 1 means no indifference exists.

explain.text: U pays $3 + q$ and D pays $2 - q$, so U is higher for every chance $q$. That is dominance, and a dominated move is never mixed in. A mix outside 0 to 1 is the signal to delete moves first.

screens.title: Make the other indifferent
screens.prose:
What you did: Ana's chance $p$ of row 1 makes Ben indifferent. So it solves an equation in **Ben's** payoffs $b_{ij}$:

$$p\,b_{11} + (1 - p)\,b_{21} = p\,b_{12} + (1 - p)\,b_{22}$$

Ben's $q$ solves the same equation in Ana's payoffs.
screens.question: Whose payoffs set Ana's mix?

options.why: That is the slip from the trap. Ana's own payoffs set Ben's mix.
Only one player's payoffs enter each equation. Ana's mix balances Ben's two columns.

hints.text: Ana's mix must keep someone indifferent.
It keeps Ben indifferent between his columns.
So it uses Ben's payoffs.

feedback.correct: Ben's: her mix balances his columns.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ana mixes to make Ben indifferent.

explain.text: Ana's $p$ balances Ben's two columns, so Ben's payoffs fix it. Ben's $q$ balances Ana's two rows. Check $0 < p < 1$; a value outside means a move is dominated.

screens.title: Drill
screens.prose: Three games, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the reasoning aloud before you answer. Give chances as fractions or decimals.

state.caption: Each row of a game lists its two cells, (Ana, Ben) in £.

screens.question: Fill in the five answers.

rows: Race: each player's chance of Aggressive
Venues: each player's chance of X
New game: Ben's chance of L

hints.text: In each game write the other player's indifference.
Race $\tfrac13$ and £2; venues $\tfrac14$ and £0.75; new game: $2q = q + 3(1 - q)$, so $q = \tfrac34$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first answer that is marked.

byKey.r3c1: Venues: X pays $3 \times \tfrac14 = 0.75$, worse than either pure equilibrium.
byKey.r4c1: Ben's $q$ makes Ana indifferent: T pays $2q$, B pays $q + 3(1 - q)$, so $q = \tfrac34$.

explain.text: Race: aggressive with chance $\tfrac13$, each expecting £2. Venues: X with chance $\tfrac14$, each expecting £0.75. New game: Ana plays T with $\tfrac12$ and Ben plays L with $\tfrac34$, each expecting £1.50.

screens.title: Follow-up: a bigger prize
screens.prose: Follow-up: the interviewer changes rock, paper, scissors. Rock beating scissors now pays £2, and costs scissors £2. Every other win still pays £1.

state.caption: Ana's winnings in £; Ben's are the same with the sign flipped.

screens.question: At the equilibrium, how often is paper played?

hints.text: Ben's mix must make rock, paper and scissors pay Ana the same.
With Ben's chances $r, p, s$: rock pays $-p + 2s$, paper $r - s$, scissors $-2r + p$.
All equal 0 with $r + p + s = 1$: $r = s = \tfrac14$, $p = \tfrac12$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make Ana's three moves pay the same against Ben's mix.

byKey.third: That is the ordinary game. The £2 prize changes the balance.
byKey.quarter: That is rock's chance, and scissors'. Paper, the answer to rock, takes the other half.

explain.text: Rock $\tfrac14$, paper $\tfrac12$, scissors $\tfrac14$ makes every move pay 0, so the value is 0. The bigger prize on rock makes paper, its answer, the most played. A trader splitting a large order at random times is mixing so a predator cannot time her.

ideas: In a mixed equilibrium each player mixes so the other is indifferent between the moves the other uses.
So Ana's chances come from Ben's payoffs, and Ben's from Ana's.
A solution outside 0 to 1 means a move is dominated: delete it first.

formula.name: Ana's mix
formula.note: Ben's payoffs, set equal across his columns.

summary.trap: Solving Ana's mix with her own payoffs. Her mix must make Ben indifferent.

quiz.prose: This game has no pure equilibrium. Ana chooses the row and Ben the column; each cell is (Ana's payoff, Ben's payoff), in £.
quiz.question: How often does Ana play T at the mixed equilibrium?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ana's mix makes Ben indifferent between L and R.

byKey.own: You made Ana indifferent with her own payoffs; that gives Ben's mix, $\tfrac34$. Use Ben's payoffs.
byKey.half: Half and half fits only a symmetric game. Solve Ben's indifference.

explain.text: Ben's L pays $3p + 1(1 - p)$ and his R pays $0 \cdot p + 2(1 - p)$. Equal when $1 + 2p = 2 - 2p$, so $p = \tfrac14$. Ben's own mix, from Ana's payoffs, is $q = \tfrac34$.

quiz.prose: Another change to rock, paper, scissors: scissors beating paper pays £3. Every other win pays £1.

state.caption: Ana's winnings in £; Ben's are the same with the sign flipped.

quiz.question: Which move is played most at the equilibrium?

options.why: You followed the bigger prize. Players answer scissors with rock, so rock is played most.
Paper loses £3 to scissors, so it is played least of all, not most.

feedback.correct: Rock: $\tfrac35$, with paper and scissors $\tfrac15$ each.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Make every move pay the same against the mix.

explain.text: With rock $\tfrac35$, paper $\tfrac15$, scissors $\tfrac15$, each move pays 0 against the mix. The big prize on scissors is held in check by extra rock. As before, the prize lifts its own answer.

quiz.prose: Ana's payoffs only: T pays 5 against L and 1 against R; B pays 2 and 0.
quiz.question: How should Ana mix between T and B?

options.why: She mixes only when indifferent. T pays more against both columns.
Payoffs do not become chances. T beats B whatever Ben does.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare T and B against each column.

explain.text: T pays more than B against L and against R. So no belief about Ben makes her indifferent. She never mixes in a dominated move.
